name: Columbia University Scholarship for Displaced Students (CUSDS)
description: The Columbia University Scholarship for Displaced Students (CUSDS) is the first university-wide scholarship initiative of its kind, providing full tuition, housing, and living assistance for up to 30 displaced students annually across all 18 Columbia schools and affiliate institutions. The program supports undergraduate and graduate degree-seekers who are foreign nationals with refugee status, internally displaced persons, asylum seekers or asylees in the United States, Afghan nationals on Humanitarian Parole, and holders of Special Immigrant Visas. CUSDS covers the full cost of attendance for the duration of terms necessary to complete the degree, removing financial barriers for students whose education has been disrupted by conflict, persecution, or forced displacement. Admitted students receive comprehensive support including academic advising, mentorship, and integration resources through Columbia's global network.
eligibility: Foreign nationals who are externally or internally displaced with refugee status; individuals who have received asylum or submitted an asylum application in the United States; displaced Afghan students on Humanitarian Parole or with Special Immigrant Visas; must meet Columbia University admissions requirements for their chosen school or program
amount: Full tuition, housing, and living expenses for the duration of the degree program
applicationProcess: Apply for admission to any of Columbia University's 18 schools or affiliate institutions through the standard admissions process. Indicate displaced student status on the application. Admitted students meeting CUSDS eligibility criteria are automatically considered for the scholarship. Contact cusds@columbia.edu for information about application periods and specific documentation requirements.
geographicScope: United States — Columbia University, New York City
documentsRequired: Proof of displacement or refugee status; standard Columbia University admissions materials (transcripts, personal statement, letters of recommendation); documentation of asylum application or refugee determination; valid identification

name: Helen Jean Simpson Scholarship for Refugee Youth (Arizona Community Foundation)
description: The Helen Jean Simpson Scholarship is administered by the Arizona Community Foundation and specifically supports youth who entered the United States with refugee status. The scholarship provides financial assistance for Arizona residents pursuing a four-year university degree, helping refugee students access higher education despite the financial and systemic barriers they often face after resettlement. Applicants must be graduating high school seniors or current undergraduates enrolled at or planning to attend a four-year university, and must maintain a minimum 3.2 GPA. The Arizona Community Foundation manages over 800 scholarship funds and has supported thousands of Arizona students, with the Helen Jean Simpson Scholarship standing as one of the few programs in the state exclusively designated for refugee students.
eligibility: Arizona residents who entered the United States with refugee status; must be a graduating high school senior or current undergraduate student; must be enrolled or planning to enroll in a four-year university; minimum 3.2 GPA required
amount: Varies by year — covers partial tuition and educational expenses
applicationProcess: Apply through the Arizona Community Foundation's online scholarship portal during the annual application period (typically opens January and closes in March). Submit academic transcripts, personal essay, letters of recommendation, and documentation of refugee status. Recipients are selected based on academic achievement, financial need, and personal statement.
geographicScope: Arizona, United States — applicants must be Arizona residents
documentsRequired: Proof of refugee status (I-94, I-571, or equivalent documentation); academic transcripts showing minimum 3.2 GPA; personal essay; letters of recommendation; proof of Arizona residency; university enrollment or acceptance confirmation

name: Alberta Trades Pathways for Newcomers Program
organization: Government of Alberta — Settlement, Integration and Language Services
description: The Alberta Trades Pathways for Newcomers program provides comprehensive trades training combined with language instruction and essential skills development for newcomers to Canada. Running from March 2025 through December 2026 in Edmonton, the program is funded through Alberta's Settlement, Integration and Language Projects grants and targets underemployed or unemployed permanent residents and convention refugees who want to enter the skilled trades workforce. Participants receive integrated vocational training, English language support contextualized to trades terminology, workplace safety certification, and hands-on experience with Alberta trade tools and standards. The program addresses a critical gap in immigrant integration by combining language acquisition with practical skills that lead directly to employment in Alberta's high-demand trades sectors including construction, electrical, plumbing, and automotive repair.
eligibility: Permanent residents of Canada or convention refugees living in Alberta; must be underemployed or unemployed; newcomers seeking entry into skilled trades; English language proficiency at CLB 4+ (intermediate level) recommended; must be legally eligible to work in Canada
amount: Fully funded — no cost to participants; includes training materials, safety equipment, and certification fees
applicationProcess: Contact the program through Alberta's Settlement, Integration and Language Projects portal or through local immigrant-serving organizations in Edmonton. Undergo a language and skills assessment to determine program fit. Enrollment is on a rolling basis while spaces are available through December 2026. Participants attend scheduled classes combining language instruction with hands-on trades training.
documentsRequired: Proof of permanent residence or convention refugee status in Canada; valid Alberta identification; language assessment results (CLB); proof of Alberta residency

name: Germany BAMF Integration Courses (Integrationskurse) for Immigrants
organization: Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) — Bundesamt für Migration und Flüchtlinge
description: Germany's Integration Courses (Integrationskurse) are the cornerstone of the country's immigrant integration policy, providing structured German language instruction and civic orientation to newcomers. Administered by the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), each course consists of up to 700 hours of German language instruction (600 hours general + 100 hours intensive for those who need it) and 100 hours of orientation covering German law, culture, history, and civic values. The courses are heavily subsidized by the German federal government: participants with social benefits pay nothing, while others contribute EUR 2.29 per lesson hour — a fraction of market rates. Successful completion leads to the B1 certificate in German, which is required for permanent residency and naturalization. BAMF authorizes approximately 1,500 course providers throughout Germany, making the program accessible in nearly every city and town. Specialized course variants are available for women, parents, young adults, and people learning to read and write.
eligibility: Newly arrived immigrants with a residence permit in Germany; EU citizens who are not yet proficient in German; recognized refugees and asylum seekers with good prospects of remaining; Spätaussiedler (ethnic German repatriates); foreigners already living in Germany who cannot communicate adequately in German; German nationals with insufficient German language skills and a migration background
amount: Heavily subsidized — free for recipients of social benefits (SGB II or asylum benefits); EUR 2.29 per lesson hour for all others (total approximately EUR 1,600 for self-payers); 50% refund if B1 exam passed within 2 years
applicationProcess: Apply at the local branch of the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) or through the Foreigners' Office (Ausländerbehörde). Receive an authorization certificate or obligation notice. Choose from approximately 1,500 authorized course providers nationwide. Take a placement test to determine starting level. Courses run full-time (morning or afternoon) or part-time (evening). Complete up to 700 hours of language instruction plus 100 hours of orientation, followed by the DTZ language exam.
geographicScope: Germany — nationwide, approximately 1,500 authorized course providers across all federal states
documentsRequired: Valid residence permit or registration certificate; authorization certificate from BAMF or obligation notice from the Foreigners' Office; passport or identity document; proof of social benefits eligibility (for fee waiver); registration at local residents' registration office (Einwohnermeldeamt)

name: IIE Scholar Rescue Fund — Emergency Fellowships for Threatened Scholars
description: The IIE Scholar Rescue Fund (IIE-SRF) provides fellowships to threatened and displaced scholars so they can continue their academic work at partner universities and research institutions worldwide. Established in 2002, the program has supported over 1,000 scholars from more than 60 countries who face threats to their lives or careers due to conflict, violence, persecution, or discrimination. Fellowships are typically awarded for one academic year, with possible renewal for a second year, and are hosted at one of 600+ partner institutions across 60 countries. Scholars receive a stipend to cover basic living expenses and may also receive supplementary support for dependents, health insurance, and research costs. The fund prioritizes scholars whose work cannot safely continue in their home country and who demonstrate a commitment to returning home or contributing to their academic community once conditions allow. IIE-SRF scholars work across all academic disciplines including science, social science, humanities, and professional fields.
eligibility: Scholars with a PhD or highest degree in their field who face direct threats to their life or career; must have a current academic appointment or recent academic affiliation; scholars from any country and any academic discipline are eligible; must be unable to safely continue their academic work in their home country due to conflict, violence, or persecution
amount: Up to $25,000 per fellowship year for stipend support; supplementary support for dependents and health insurance may be available; fellowships typically last one academic year with possible renewal
applicationProcess: Submit an application through the IIE Scholar Rescue Fund online portal at scholarrescuefund.org. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis with no fixed deadline. Include a detailed description of the threats faced, academic CV, research proposal, and letters of recommendation. IIE reviews applications and matches selected scholars with host institutions from its global network of 600+ partner universities. Scholars may also be nominated by university faculty, academic associations, or human rights organizations.
geographicScope: International — fellowships hosted at 600+ partner institutions across 60+ countries; IIE headquarters in New York, United States
documentsRequired: PhD or equivalent degree documentation; detailed CV or resume; description of threats or persecution faced; research proposal for fellowship period; letters of recommendation from academic colleagues; passport or identity documentation; proof of most recent academic appointment
